messages.subject: drc, ddply and  doSMP no improvement?
parts:
Dear people I would like to use parallel computing in combination with
ddply using
the doSMP package.
My dataset consitst of a set of (1240) dose (x) response (y) curves
that can be mapped by factors
rowSeq and colSeq. (11 doses each in duplicate hence 22 datapoints per
curve.
I would like to fit curves using the drm function in the drc package.
Code would look like this:

library(drc)
fitfunction<-function(dataset){
x=dataset$x
y=dataset$y
#perform regression
model<-try(model<-drm(y~x,data=dataset,fct=LL.4(),
na.action=na.omit) , silent=TRUE)
if (!inherits(model, "try-error")){
HillSlope<-coef(model)[1]
bottom<-coef(model)[2]
top<-coef(model)[3]
logEC50<-log10(coef(model)[4])
}else{
HillSlope<-0
bottom<-mean(y)
top<-mean(y)
logEC50<-max(x)+2
}

r <- c(HillSlope,bottom,top,logEC50)
return(r)}


Fitting the dataset :

library(plyr)
system.time(ddply(dataset,~colSeq+rowSeq,fitfunction))

results in :
user system elapsed
107.73 0.66 108.39

Now by parallel computation, using doSMP:

library(doSMP)
workers <- startWorkers(2) # My computer has 2 cores
registerDoSMP(workers)
system.time(ddply(dataset,~colSeq+rowSeq, fitfunction,.parallel=TRUE))
stopWorkers(workers)

results in:
user system elapsed
107.93 0.51 108.50

Virtually the same time???
What am I doing wrong? Why is it not faster? Am I missing something?

Thanks
Rene

ps. I would like to upload my dataset, where can I do that?

Can I ask why you think there should be a difference? I mean, on
your particular computer, are there other programs for which the R
multicore functionality makes a substantial difference?

For me, on a dual core system, I usually see almost no effect with
multicore applications. OS and R are occupying one core, even though
you try to give 2 cores, the multicore system doesn't actually have
access to 2 completely separate cores. But it tries to use 2, and it
has a lot of frustration trying.

If you are on an 8 core system, and you set aside 2 for multicore, I'm
a little surprised. If you have 8 cores, and 1 has the OS, 1 has R and
plyr, then the regression calculations could get sent to idle cores.

In an 8 core system, I recently conducted a lot of stress testing and
found that some test programs ran slower as more cores were
allocated. In most testing, about 1/2 of the cores was the optimum
number to set aside. I'm not an engineer, I have no good way of
knowing if the explanations I get from people are good or not. Some
are more-or-less believable, such as "you have 8 CPU, but not 8
separate paths from CPU to RAM, so there's a log jam," or "you have
one data set, it can't go 8 places at once" or "you have 8 CPU, but
the decision making required to separate the work and send it out
slows the whole thing down."

Like many people, I expected multicore to work like a "magic bullet"
and make everything go two times as fast. Sending separate jobs
across systems, well, is usually substantially faster.

Oh, one more thing. Even if you don't run with the parallel option,
it may be that your BLAS is doing the parallel work for you.
GOTOBlas2, for example, will split matrix calculations and use as many
threads as it can grab. So explicitly telling R to separate the
calculations may have no effect at all. It may even get slower, as
there is confusion as the separate components fight for control of
your cores.

pj

--
Paul E. Johnson

linearly reduces the calculation time with the number of cores, as

load('dataset.rdata')

function(...) Sys.sleep(0.05)))
